title: The Window · 8
paragraphs: He made no answer. He took opium. According to the children, it had stained his beard yellow. Perhaps it had. What was plain to her was that the poor man was unhappy, and that he came to them every year to escape; and still, every year, she felt the same thing: he did not trust her. She would say, “I’m going into town. Can I get you stamps, paper, tobacco?” and feel him flinch. He did not trust her. His wife was to blame. She remembered the wicked way his wife had treated him, which had turned her, Mrs. Ramsay, to steel and adamant right there in that horrid little room in St. John’s Wood, when she had watched with her own eyes as that hateful woman turned him out of the house. He was untidy; he spilled things on his coat; he had all the tedious habits of an old man with nothing in the world to do; and his wife turned him out of the room. In her hateful way she said, “Now, Mrs. Ramsay and I want to have a little talk together,” and Mrs. Ramsay could see, as clearly as if they were before her eyes, the endless miseries of his life. Had he enough money for tobacco? Did he have to ask his wife for it? Half a crown? Eighteen pence? Oh, she could not bear to think of the small humiliations that woman put him through. And always now (she could not guess why, unless it came from that woman somehow) he shrank away from her. He never confided in her. Yet what more could she have done? A sunny room had been set aside for him. The children were kind to him. Not once had she shown any sign that he was unwelcome. In fact she went out of her way to be friendly. Do you want stamps, do you want tobacco? Here’s a book you might enjoy, and so on. And after all—after all (at this point, without being aware of it, she drew herself up, and the sense of her own beauty, so seldom present to her, came to her now)—after all, she did not usually find it hard to make people like her. There was George Manning, for example; Mr. Wallace; famous men though they were, they would come to see her in the evening, quietly, and talk with her alone by her fire. She could not help knowing that she carried the torch of her beauty with her wherever she went; she carried it high into every room she walked into. And after all, however much she might veil it, and shrink from the monotonous bearing it forced on her, her beauty showed. She had been admired. She had been loved. She had walked into rooms where people sat mourning. Tears had been shed in front of her. Men, and women too, had set aside the multitude of things in their lives and allowed themselves, with her, the relief of simplicity. It wounded her that he should shrink from her. It hurt. And yet it was not a clean hurt, not a right one. That was what bothered her, coming as it did on top of her discontent with her husband: the feeling she had now—as Mr. Carmichael shuffled past, barely nodding in answer to her question, a book under his arm, in his yellow slippers—that she was under suspicion; that all this longing of hers to give, to help, was vanity. Was it for her own gratification that she wanted so instinctively to help, to give, so that people would say of her, “O Mrs. Ramsay! dear Mrs. Ramsay … Mrs. Ramsay, of course!” and need her, and send for her, and admire her? Wasn’t this what she secretly wanted? And so when Mr. Carmichael drew back from her, as he was doing at this very moment, slipping away to some corner where he did his acrostic puzzles endlessly, she felt not simply rebuffed in her instinct, but made aware of the pettiness of some part of herself, and of human relations—how flawed they are, how contemptible, how selfish, even at their best. Worn out and shabby, and presumably no longer (her cheeks were hollow, her hair was white) a sight to fill anyone’s eyes with joy, she had better give her mind to the story of the Fisherman and his Wife, and so calm that bundle of sensitiveness, her son James (none of her children was as sensitive as he was).

“The man’s heart grew heavy,” she read aloud, “and he did not want to go. ‘It is not right,’ he said to himself, but he went all the same. And when he reached the sea, the water was all purple and dark blue, and gray and thick, not green and yellow the way it had been, but it was still calm. And he stood there and said—”

Mrs. Ramsay could have wished her husband hadn’t picked that moment to stop. Why hadn’t he gone off to watch the children play cricket, as he’d said he would? But he said nothing; he looked; he nodded; he approved; he moved on. Before him he saw the hedge that had so many times rounded off a pause, signaled a conclusion; he saw his wife and child; he saw once more the urns with their trailing red geraniums, which had so often decorated his processes of thought and which bore them written up among their leaves, like scraps of paper you scribble notes on in the rush of reading. Seeing all this, he slid smoothly into speculation prompted by an article in _The Times_ on how many Americans visit Shakespeare’s house each year. Had Shakespeare never existed, he asked, would the world be much different from the way it is now? Does civilization advance because of great men? Is the ordinary person better off now than under the Pharaohs? And yet, he asked himself, is the ordinary person’s lot the right yardstick for measuring civilization? Possibly not. Possibly the greatest good depends on there being a slave class. The man who operates the lift in the Underground will always be necessary. He found the thought distasteful. He tossed his head. To escape it, he would find a way to take the arts down a peg. He would argue that the world exists for the ordinary person; that the arts are just ornament laid on top of human life; they do not express it. Nor does life need Shakespeare. Without knowing quite why he wanted to run Shakespeare down and to rescue the man who stands forever in the door of the lift, he snapped a leaf off the hedge. All this would have to be served up for the young men at Cardiff next month, he thought; out here on his terrace he was only foraging and picnicking (he tossed away the leaf he had picked so peevishly), like a man leaning down from his horse to gather a bunch of roses, or filling his pockets with nuts as he ambles comfortably through the lanes and fields of the countryside he has known since he was a boy. All of it was familiar: this bend, that stile, that path across the fields. He would spend hours this way in the evenings, with his pipe, thinking his way up and down and in and out of the old familiar lanes and commons, which were all dotted with the history of that campaign over there, the life of this statesman here, with poems and anecdotes, and with figures too, this thinker, that soldier; everything brisk and clear. But eventually the lane, the field, the common, the fruitful nut tree and the flowering hedge brought him to that further bend in the road where he always dismounted, tied his horse to a tree, and went on alone, on foot. He came to the edge of the lawn and gazed out over the bay below.

It was his fate, his particular nature, whether he liked it or not, to come out like this onto a spit of land that the sea is slowly eating away, and to stand there by himself like some desolate seabird. It was his power, his gift, to throw off everything superfluous all at once, shrinking and dwindling until he looked barer and felt leaner, even in his body, yet without losing any of the intensity of his mind; and in that state to stand on his little ledge, facing the darkness of human ignorance—how we know nothing, and the sea eats away the ground we stand on. That was his fate, his gift. But when he dismounted he had cast off every gesture and frill, all his trophies of nuts and roses, and had shrunk until he had forgotten not only his fame but his very name; and even in that desolation he stayed alert, sparing no phantom, indulging in no vision. And it was in this guise that he inspired a deep reverence, and pity, and gratitude as well, in William Bankes (now and then), in Charles Tansley (fawningly), and in his wife now, as she looked up and saw him standing at the edge of the lawn. It was the kind of gratitude that a stake, driven into the bed of a channel, with gulls perching on it and waves beating against it, inspires in boatloads of merrymakers, for the duty it has taken on of marking the channel out there in the floods, alone.

“But the father of eight children has no choice. …” He broke off his half-audible muttering, turned, sighed, lifted his eyes, looked for the figure of his wife reading stories to the little boy, and filled his pipe. He turned his back on the sight of human ignorance and human fate and the sea eating the ground we stand on—a sight which, had he been able to hold his gaze on it, might have led somewhere. And he took comfort in trifles so slight, next to the grand theme he had just been facing, that he was inclined to skip over that comfort, to disown it, as though for an honest man to be caught being happy in a world of misery were the most shameful crime of all. It was true: most of the time he was happy; he had his wife; he had his children; in six weeks he had promised to talk “some nonsense” to the young men of Cardiff about Locke, Hume, Berkeley, and the causes of the French Revolution. But all this, and the pleasure he took in it—in the phrases he turned, in the ardor of the young, in his wife’s beauty, in the tributes that came to him from Swansea, Cardiff, Exeter, Southampton, Kidderminster, Oxford, Cambridge—all of it had to be made light of and hidden under the words “talking nonsense,” because, in effect, he had not done the thing he might have done. It was a disguise. It was where a man took refuge who was afraid to own his own feelings, who could not say, This is what I like—this is what I am. And William Bankes and Lily Briscoe found it rather pitiful and distasteful; they wondered why such concealments were needed; why he always needed praise; why a man so brave in his thinking should be so timid in his living; how oddly he was both venerable and laughable at once.

Lily suspected that teaching and preaching are more than any human being can manage. (She was packing up her things.) If you are lifted up high, you are bound to come down with a crash somehow. Mrs. Ramsay gave him what he wanted too easily. And then the change must be so jarring, Lily said. He comes in from his books and finds us all playing games and chattering nonsense. Just think what a change that is from the things he thinks about, she said.
He was bearing down on them. Now he had stopped dead and was standing, silent, looking out at the sea. Now he had turned away again.
